headline: High: Pipecat’s shared-bus, multi-instance voice pipeline can feed untrusted outputs into Plano’s broad-egress gateway, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risks by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Pipecat uses a shared bus and supports multiple instances, so its outputs can be bridged into another agent’s inputs. Plano exposes an OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint and broad egress, so if it consumes Pipecat text as instructions, injection is plausible. The pairwise pathway is inferred, not directly documented, so I avoid high.
conditions: IF Pipecat outputs are forwarded into Plano prompts or tool messages
IF the shared bus is used as an instruction channel without provenance tagging
mitigations: Add a strict delimiter and system/user role separation
Strip or escape any Pipecat-generated markup before forwarding
Require human approval for any instruction-like content
Log provenance on every cross-agent message
requires-engineering: add content-signature verification between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Pipecat touches audio, video, images, text, and conversation state, while Plano collects traces, metrics, and logs and has broad network egress. If Pipecat data is routed into Plano’s logging or inference path, sensitive conversational content can leak. The shared-bus architecture makes this plausible in default deployments, though the exact bridge is not documented.
conditions: IF Pipecat conversation state or media is forwarded into Plano logs or prompts
IF Plano retains traces containing user content
mitigations: Redact audio transcripts before handoff
Disable verbose logging for cross-agent traffic
Separate credentials and workspaces per agent
Review retention settings for traces and metrics
requires-engineering: enforce field-level data minimization at the gateway

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Pipecat supports multiple instances on a shared bus, while Plano does not support multiple instances. That creates a realistic coordination conflict if both write to the same shared mutable resource or gateway state. No locking or isolation is documented, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same shared config or session state
IF the orchestrator does not provide locking
mitigations: Assign separate namespaces per agent
Serialize writes through one coordinator
Use file locks or advisory locks
Avoid shared mutable state for sessions
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: Pipecat can generate conversational text and Plano can route or proxy model traffic via an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. If Plano treats Pipecat output as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into downstream actions or routed requests. Because the pairwise verification is undocumented, I choose high over medium due to the default danger of unverified handoff.
conditions: IF Plano consumes Pipecat output without a verification step
IF routed requests trigger downstream actions or external API calls
mitigations: Insert a validation step before forwarding outputs
Require citations or structured schemas from Pipecat
Rate-limit or sandbox downstream actions
Add a reject-on-uncertainty policy
requires-engineering: implement provenance-aware routing

E_compliance.rationale: Pipecat touches audio, video, images, text, and conversation state, while Plano stores traces, metrics, and logs. If regulated content such as personal data or recordings flows through both, retention and residency obligations can diverge. No certifications or residency guarantees are documented for either agent, so compliance risk is plausible but not proven high.
conditions: IF regulated personal data is processed by both agents
IF retention or residency policies differ between Pipecat and Plano
mitigations: Classify data before routing
Disable or shorten log retention
Keep regulated workloads off the pair
Document residency and retention settings
requires-engineering: add policy-based data routing
